tip: 'Gato escaldado', a scalded cat, carries the once bitten, twice shy idea: one bad burn leaves you wary of even harmless cold water.
'Deixar de' plus an infinitive means to stop doing something. 'Ela deixou de responder' = she stopped answering.
'Embargo' here isn't a trade ban. 'Sem embargo de' is a formal legal phrase meaning notwithstanding or in spite of.
'Em' plus an '-ndo' form, as in 'em sendo assim', is literally in being so, a formal pattern English rarely builds.
'Não fossem' plus a noun means were it not for. 'Não fossem as circunstâncias' = if it weren't for the circumstances.
In Antônio Conselheiro's famous prophecy, 'virar' is the everyday become-verb: 'virar mar' means to turn into sea.
'Oxalá' means hopefully or may it be, and it always triggers the subjunctive. That is why the verb is 'colham', not 'colhem'.
'Gonzagão' adds the '-ão' ending to 'Gonzaga', the 'baião' king, giving big Gonzaga, an affectionate size-up Portuguese applies to people.
'Vossa Excelência' takes a third-person verb, so it goes with 'está', not 'estás', even though you address one person.
The pattern 'haver de' plus an infinitive expresses expectation about the future. 'Não há de ser fácil' = it won't be easy.
Here 'vir' is the future subjunctive of 'ver' (to see), not the verb 'vir' (to come). 'Quando eu o vir' = when I see him.
In 'far-se-á' the pronoun 'se' sits inside the future verb, splitting 'fará' open. This ultra-formal split is written and legal, hardly ever spoken.
'Prejuízo' usually means loss or harm, not prejudice, which is 'preconceito'. Yet 'sem prejuízo de' is legal Portuguese for without prejudice to.
